title: People really hate AI, so why can’t they get enough?
gist: Public sentiment toward AI is souring sharply in polls even as usage hits record highs (ChatGPT at 1 billion monthly users). The author argues the dislike targets the companies' relentless pushing and apocalyptic framing, not the technology, and sees regulation and open-source alternatives as possible checks.

insights.claim: More US adults expect AI to have a negative impact on them personally and on society than expect a positive one, with pessimism strongest among the young.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Negative consumer sentiment among the young is a long-run demand and political risk for AI vendors.

insights.claim: More than half of people worldwide say AI products and services make them nervous, per a Stanford report.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Nervousness is global, not just a US phenomenon.
insights.locator: More than half of people worldwide

insights.claim: In a May Gallup poll, 71% of US adults opposed a new AI data center in their area, versus 53% who opposed a new nuclear power plant.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Local opposition to data centers raises siting, permitting and cost risk for AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.locator: In a Gallup poll in May

insights.claim: In a March NBC poll, AI was less popular than ICE.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: AI is politically toxic enough to be a campaign target.
insights.locator: And in an NBC poll in March

insights.claim: ChatGPT reached a billion monthly users in May, and Google's Gemini logged 950 million users in July, per Sensor Tower.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Chatbot distribution is consolidating around two giants with near-parity scale.
insights.locator: Yet the number of people using AI

insights.claim: Half of US adults now use a chatbot, more than twice the 2023 share, and one in four use one daily.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Adoption has crossed into mass-market habit despite negative sentiment.
insights.locator: According to Pew, half of US adults

insights.claim: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries used generative AI tools in the last three months.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Adoption is broad across rich economies.

insights.claim: The author doubts that haters and users are separate groups; the numbers only add up if the overlap is close to a full circle, so the same people both dislike and use AI.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Stated attitudes are a weak predictor of usage, so sentiment polls should not be read as demand signals.
insights.quote: The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.
insights.locator: It’s possible that these are two distinct groups

insights.claim: Usage may breed negativity: the Global North, with the highest adoption, skews pessimistic, while the lower-adoption Global South is more optimistic.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Emerging markets may offer friendlier demand and politics, though sentiment could sour as adoption rises.
insights.locator: It’s also possible that the more people use AI

insights.claim: The author's main thesis is that people dislike not the technology but the companies' relentless drive to push it everywhere, while warning of the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Apocalyptic marketing by AI labs may be fueling backlash; more modest positioning could ease it.
insights.locator: But here’s what I really think

insights.claim: AI is following the social media and Google search pattern of mass usage despite mounting techlash against the companies behind them.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Historically, techlash has not dented usage or incumbents' economics.
insights.locator: In many ways, we’ve been here before

insights.claim: Unlike social media, where network lock-in made quitting costly, AI users face lower switching costs, leaving more room for consumer influence.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Weak lock-in implies chatbot share is contestable and pricing power is limited.
insights.locator: With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do

insights.claim: All 50 US states have passed or proposed AI laws, a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills, a tenfold increase in three years.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Rising compliance fragmentation and regulatory risk for AI developers and deployers.

insights.claim: Top-class open-source alternatives to Google, OpenAI and Anthropic already exist, offering for now the potential for consumer choice and market pressure.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Open-source competition caps proprietary labs' pricing and narrative power.

insights.claim: The author argues the future is not as inevitable as AI companies imply and hopes for clearer messaging on what AI can and cannot do, without sales pitches that it will take over the world.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: A shift from AGI hype to realistic positioning could change how AI is sold and valued.
insights.locator: I don’t want to be naïve

insights.claim: The CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that produces a wider variety of responses than mainstream rivals, calls it a self-loathing AI company and says there is no walking back from LLMs, only making them do something different.
insights.speaker: Will Douglas Heaven
insights.so_what: Even builders are ambivalent, and differentiation via response diversity is an emerging niche.
insights.quote: We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company.
insights.locator: Over the summer I talked to the CEO
